title: Head in the Cloud? What's on the Horizon for Offline Intelligence
blurb: Subscription fatigue? There should be an app for that. Explores the consequences of cloud-based assistive technology delivery — the subscription trap, recurring cost burden, and what offline and on-device AI alternatives exist today and on the horizon.

featured_slides.note: LiveScribe is a useful case study because it illustrates the trajectory so clearly — the intelligence starts on the device, then the subscription creep begins as the cloud becomes load-bearing. The note paper itself becomes the recurring revenue mechanism.

The Kurzweil Reading Machine is the origin point of the whole conversation. Purpose-built, expensive, offline, no recurring cost — and genuinely transformative for blind readers. The question the talk asks is whether anything in that model is recoverable.

The ImageNet moment is where the current AI wave actually began. The 2012 AlexNet result wasn't just an incremental improvement — it was a discontinuity that made everything that followed possible, including the on-device models the talk ends with.

The Epoch AI chart makes the case that algorithmic progress — not just raw compute — is driving capability gains. This matters for the offline argument: if you can do more with less, on-device becomes viable at the consumer hardware level.

Small is Sufficient is the thesis slide in chart form. The trend across every modality — language, vision, audio — is that the smallest model capable of a given task keeps shrinking. That compression is what makes offline assistive technology plausible again.
